summary: This experimental RFC extends RFC 7182, which defines Integrity Check Values for packets and messages in the format of RFC 5444, by adding a cryptographic function creating an ICV that is an Identity-Based Signature, for MANET routing protocols.

plainLanguage.summary: A way for wireless ad hoc network devices to sign routing messages with a signature tied to their identity.

questions: how do manet routers authenticate messages
what is an identity based signature
how does key management work in ad hoc networks
subtitle: A way for wireless ad hoc networks to sign routing messages with identity-based signatures.

tldr.problem: Mobile ad hoc network (MANET) routing protocols need to authenticate messages, but existing methods either use symmetric keys (creating a single point of failure) or require a public key infrastructure with certificates.
tldr.mechanism: This specification extends RFC 7182 by defining two new integrity check functions based on identity-based signatures (IBS) using the ECCSI algorithm from RFC 6507. A router's identity can be its network address, optionally combined with additional key-id data.
tldr.outcome: Routers can verify not just that a message is valid, but also who originated it, enabling revocation and reducing the damage from a compromised router. The specification is experimental pending wider implementation and public security analysis.

today: RFC 7859 is experimental. It has been implemented for OLSRv2 networks and is part of standards like ETSI LTE ProSe, but there are limited independent reports of use and public analysis. It remains open for feedback from implementation and deployment experience.

sections.title: Authentication in Ad Hoc Networks
sections.content:
Mobile ad hoc networks (MANETs) route messages when nodes move in and out of range. Routing protocols must verify that a message is valid and has not been corrupted. RFC 7182 defines a framework for Integrity Check Values (ICVs) appended to MANET packets and messages.

This specification adds a new cryptographic function that creates an ICV using an Identity-Based Signature (IBS). Unlike a simple integrity check (which only detects corruption), an IBS proves who created the message. This matters for MANET security: if a router is compromised or revoked, the network can reject all messages from that identity.

The IBS implementation used here is ECCSI (Elliptic Curve-Based Certificateless Signatures for Identity-Based Encryption), specified in RFC 6507. A trusted authority called the Key Management Service (KMS) issues each router a private key once, tied to that router's identity. The router then signs messages without needing the KMS again.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of everyone sharing one key (risky if it leaks) or carrying certificates (bulky), each router gets a private key from a trusted authority. It can then sign its messages forever to prove it is the real router.

sections.title: Identity-Based Signatures and ECCSI
sections.content:
ECCSI is based on elliptic curve mathematics. The Key Management Service holds a master secret and uses it to generate a unique private key for each router. A router's identity is typically its network address (IP source address or message originator address), optionally combined with a key-id field that might encode an expiry time.

The signature length depends on the security level: for 128-bit security, the signature is 129 octets (32-byte address plus coordinate plus overhead). This is longer than symmetric checksums like HMAC-SHA-256 (32 octets), reflecting the added cryptographic work.

Unlike RSA or ECDSA, ECCSI does not use public key certificates or require routers to maintain each other's keys. Each router only needs the KMS's public key (the KPAK). During normal MANET operation, the KMS does not need to be present; it is used only to issue keys initially.

The disadvantage is the trusted authority problem: the KMS has complete authority and could impersonate any router through its master secret. This is a trade-off for the simpler key management.
sections.plainLanguage: ECCSI is like a fingerprint reader that needs one setup visit to the authority, then works offline forever. The downside is the authority is very powerful: it could fake anyone's fingerprint.

sections.title: The ECCSI Cryptographic Functions
sections.content:
This specification defines two code points for ECCSI functions in RFC 7182's ICV registry. They differ in how identity is formed:

ECCSI (code 7): The identity is the element key-id from the ICV, which must not be empty. This allows arbitrary identity data per message.

ECCSI-ADDR (code 8): The identity is an address (IP source address, message originator address, or message sender address) concatenated with the key-id, which may be empty. This allows the router's network address to be part of the signature automatically.

The hash function used must produce a fixed-length output N (determined by the elliptic curve parameters). For 128-bit security with the recommended P-256 curve, N is 32 octets and SHA-256 is the hash function.

Verification is not done by recalculating the signature; instead, the receiver evaluates the verify function from RFC 6507 against the received ICV-value. A router may be configured to reject ECCSI signatures based on the key-id (for example, if it encodes an expiry time that has passed).
sections.plainLanguage: There are two variants: one uses a custom identity in the message, and one automatically includes the router's address. Both create signatures that prove the router's identity.

sections.title: Applicability and Use in Routing Protocols
sections.content:
This specification is applicable to MANET routing protocols that use RFC 5444 format packets and messages with RFC 7182 ICVs. Specific examples mentioned are the Neighborhood Discovery Protocol (NHDP, RFC 6130) and the Optimized Link State Routing Protocol Version 2 (OLSRv2, RFC 7181), both expected users of this extension.

The ECCSI-ADDR variant is recommended for most cases, as it automatically binds the signature to the originating router's address. A router with multiple identities may use different key-ids for each. Routers must be administratively configured with the same elliptic curve parameters (such as P-256 from NIST FIPS 186-4).

The computational load is non-trivial: ECCSI signature and verification involve elliptic curve point operations. Implementation performance depends on the quality of the elliptic curve library. Unlike some other IBS methods, ECCSI does not use 'pairings' (bilinear maps), which may make it easier to implement and more efficient in some contexts.
sections.plainLanguage: MANET routing protocols like OLSR can use ECCSI to sign their control messages. All routers must agree on which curve to use, and the computation is heavier than older methods but simpler than some alternatives.

sections.title: Security, Trust, and Experimental Status
sections.content:
The main security advantage over symmetric ICVs (like HMAC) is that a compromised router's key cannot decrypt everything; it can only forge messages from that one identity. Key revocation is possible by blacklist or time expiry encoded in the key-id.

The main security advantage over traditional public-key signatures (RSA, ECDSA) is simplicity: no certificates, no certificate authority, and routers need not keep key material for other routers. A router can be keyed independently of others.

The main security risk is the trusted KMS: it has access to all private keys and could impersonate any router. This is acceptable in environments where the KMS is physically and administratively secure. For environments where the KMS cannot be trusted, this approach is not suitable.

This specification was published as Experimental because, although ECCSI is based on sound mathematics and is used in standards like ETSI LTE ProSe, there are limited reports of use in MANET routing, and there have been no independent public security analyses of ECCSI in this context. The intent is to encourage implementation and field experience.
sections.plainLanguage: ECCSI is more secure than a shared key but relies on trusting a central authority forever. It is new enough to this application that we are still learning if it works well in real networks.
